summary: Japanese angelica tree is a fast-growing shrub or tree that can reach almost 40 feet, growing up to two feet in a season. It has very large, fern-like leaves and stems covered in sharp spines. It forms dense stands whose shade crowds out native shrubs and wildflowers, and one plant can quickly spread into a large colony. The tree grows in disturbed woods and edges such as old fields, thickets and hedgerows.
history: Japanese angelica tree is native to East Asia and has only recently arrived in the Northeast. Because it is still a fairly new invader to this region, scientists don't yet know much about how quickly it reproduces.
seasons: Japanese angelica tree produces large, flat clusters of white flowers in July and August that can reach two feet across, making it easy to identify during this time. Small purple to black berries typically develop by September.

handling.text: Young plants can be pulled or dug up before they make seed; larger plants tend to resprout from roots left in the ground. Managed areas should be checked for several years for new seedlings. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
